title: HuMI: Robot-Free Demonstrations with Online Humanoid Feasibility Feedback
content_lines: Source: [arXiv:2602.06643v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06643v2). No public training implementation was available at the audited point; the mapping below is therefore limited to the paper's declared system interfaces.

> **Bottom line:** HuMI lets a human demonstrate without wearing or directly teleoperating the robot, while a humanoid-conditioned interface feeds feasibility back to the demonstrator. The value is the closed data-collection loop, not a claim that unconstrained human video automatically becomes executable robot motion.
## Engineering problem

Robot demonstrations are expensive and risky, while unconstrained human demonstrations often contain reaches, balance states, and timing that the target humanoid cannot execute. Offline filtering discovers those failures only after collection.
## Method

HuMI couples human motion capture, target-humanoid adaptation, online feasibility feedback, action chunks, and downstream policy learning. The demonstrator changes behavior in response to the robot-aware interface, so data quality is improved during acquisition rather than only by deleting samples later.

## Decisive evidence

The useful comparison is not merely task success; it is whether robot-aware feedback changes the collected demonstrations and reduces downstream infeasibility or drift. That is the mechanism the ablation must support.
## Paper-to-implementation mapping

Because official code was not public, this brief does not invent symbols. A faithful implementation must expose timestamped human observations, robot-feasibility feedback, chunk boundaries, policy observations/actions, reset decisions, and the exact transformation from interface output to robot command.
## Limits and evidence boundary

The interface still depends on sensing, calibration, and a target-specific feasibility model. Human adaptation can bias the collected behavior toward what the current model accepts. Evidence for the reported platform and tasks cannot be generalized to arbitrary robots, objects, or safety-critical contact.
## Bounded engineering takeaway

Use online feasibility feedback when collection cost is high and offline rejection would waste many demonstrations. Preserve both rejected and accepted segments with reasons so the interface does not silently narrow the task distribution.
## Reproduction checklist

Lock calibration, coordinate frames, target robot, feedback latency, chunk horizon, dataset split, policy inputs, and reset logic. Report collection time, rejection/repair rate, operator adaptation, task success, drift, intervention count, and representative failures.
